summary:
The District of Columbia stands under the national framework of the United States, and federal executive orders and agency actions apply directly within the District because it is the federal seat. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places the District of Columbia on its Low-Risk list alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, while cautioning that the District may no longer warrant its prior reputation as the most protective jurisdiction, because District law can be overridden by congressional action and by executive orders.

Congress exercises direct legislative authority over the District, and has used it to attach a bathroom ban to District legislation. Transgender-rights activists were arrested on 5 December 2024 while protesting at the Capitol against that bathroom ban, an incident that shows congressional intervention in District facilities rules and the arrest exposure attached to opposing it.

Because the District has no state government of its own in the ordinary sense, the federal measures described in the national record — passport marker restrictions, entry screening markings, federal facility bans, custody policies, and care restrictions — operate on visitors in the District without any intervening state layer to soften them.
tangentialFactors:
The District's position is unusual among United States jurisdictions: its protective ordinances exist at the pleasure of Congress, which can amend or repeal them without District consent, and federal executive orders take effect immediately within its borders. The July 2026 assessment's caution about the District reflects that structural exposure rather than any District-specific statute.

The District appears in the same low-risk grouping as several states with protective statutes, but the mechanism differs: those states hold their protections under state constitutions, whereas the District holds ordinances subject to congressional review.
localsOnly: Residents of the District live under ordinances that Congress can modify, and the December 2024 arrests at the Capitol followed a protest against a congressional bathroom ban attached to District legislation, indicating that local facilities rules have already been a site of direct congressional intervention.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific text and current operative status of the congressional bathroom ban attached to District legislation is not sourced in the inventory; only the December 2024 protest and arrests against it are documented here.

Whether the District's own local government has enacted or retained any trans-specific protections beyond what the July 2026 assessment implies is unresolved in this inventory.
